subject: Aligning TTFT & streaming handshake for NimbleHealth pilot

From: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>

Subject: Aligning TTFT & streaming handshake for NimbleHealth pilot

Hi Samira / Alex — thanks again for the call today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have a single source of truth on the perf SLOs and streaming behavior for the pilot: 

Summary of your asks / constraints
- Primary: Time-to-first-token (TTFT) SLOs for short chat responses (~<=32 tokens): median <= 80 ms, p95 <= 200 ms.
- Longer completions (~>32 tokens / avg ~120 tokens): median ~120 ms, p95 <= 350 ms.
- Streaming preference: Server-Sent Events (SSE) as first choice for simplicity; accept WebSocket as fallback in case of restrictive client infra.
- Chunk cadence: you want the first chunk streamed within the TTFT SLO, followed by 1–3 subsequent chunks for short messages (aiming to keep per-chunk payloads small to avoid buffering delays). Heartbeat/keepalive every ~10s for long-lived streams.
- Concurrency / throughput: expect steady-state ~2k rps (concurrent open streams + request starts), peak bursts up to ~5k for marketing spikes. Average tokens per request estimated ~40; peak token throughput estimate ~200k tokens/sec.

What Redwood proposes (high level)
- Run an initial synthetic probe (we can schedule as soon as we have sample payloads and an allowlist entry for our probe IPs). Probe will exercise SSE and WebSocket handshakes, measure cold / warm TTFT, and collect p50/p95/p99.
- Use dedicated inference pool for the pilot (pins model version, consistent latency). We'll enable continuous batching tuned to keep median TTFT under target while respecting p95.
- Prefix (KV) caching for the few high-frequency prompts you mentioned to reduce per-request compute.
- Fallback routing: if SSE handshake fails or the client reports environmental limits, route to WebSocket endpoint automatically.

Open questions we need from you
1) Confirm a realistic peak concurrency number during your go-live window (is 5k burst a hard ceiling or an extreme)?
2) Share 100 sample requests (payloads + expected token distribution) so our probe mirrors production.
3) Can you add service_account@nimblehealth.com to the allowlist for synthetic probes?

Next steps & owners
- Jordan: schedule probe window and share Redwood probe IPs (ETA: Mon 6/21)
- Karthik: prepare probe config and initial performance baseline (ETA: Tue 6/22)
- Priya: produce pilot runbook + success criteria doc; add fallback routing config (ETA: Tue 6/22)
- Samira/Alex: share sample payloads, confirm allowlist entry for nimble service account (ETA: EOD Mon 6/21)

Attachments: nimble_latency_probe_results.csv (sample synthetic results from a small sandbox run), nimble_api_schema_v2.pdf (your API schema you emailed during the call)

Thanks — will follow up with calendar invites for a 90-min pilot kickoff once we have the payloads.

—Jordan

- We prefer SSE for browser clients; server teams may use WebSockets for internal batch processors.
- Primary region: us-east-1.

Internal notes — quick tech read: 
- With a dedicated pool and KV prefix caching for the top 10 prompts, hitting median <=80ms for short responses is achievable on gpus with optimized kernels (we should target a 2–3 token priming chunk to reach first byte quickly).
- p95 pressure comes from queuing at model entry and from heavy tokenization on large system prompts; we should test two configs: (A) lean prompt + prefix cache, (B) full prompt no cache. Probe should include both.
- Concurrency plan: autoscale ramp at 60% CPU/GPU utilization; reserve headroom for 3k sustained and allow immediate burst to 5k using prewarmed instances.
- For SSE vs WS: handshake overhead is similar; SSE simplifies client reconnection semantics. We'll implement a 250ms handshake budget inside the probe assertions for both.

I'll prepare the probe config (token distribution, warm/cold flows, handshake timing). Need the sample payloads & allowlist.

—Karthik
Principal Infra Engineer
